claim: The study analyzed multimodal magnetic resonance imaging data from 439 participants aged 5.7–21.9 years.
source: We used multimodal magnetic resonance imaging data from 439 participants aged 5.7–21.9 years to predict functional connectivity by incorporating intracortical and extracortical structural connectivity, characterizing SC–FC coupling.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size and age range in the abstract.

claim: SC–FC coupling was strongest in the visual and somatomotor networks.
source: Our findings revealed that SC–FC coupling was strongest in the visual and somatomotor networks, consistent with evolutionary expansion, myelin content, and functional principal gradient.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: SC–FC coupling exhibited heterogeneous alterations dominated by an increase in cortical regions during development.
source: As development progressed, SC–FC coupling exhibited heterogeneous alterations dominated by an increase in cortical regions, broadly distributed across the somatomotor, frontoparietal, dorsal attention, and default mode networks.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes developmental changes, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: SC–FC coupling significantly predicted individual variability in general intelligence.
source: Moreover, we discovered that SC–FC coupling significantly predicted individual variability in general intelligence, mainly influencing frontoparietal and default mode networks.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, supported by predictive modeling results in Figure 4.

claim: The heterogeneous development of SC–FC coupling is positively associated with genes in oligodendrocyte-related pathways.
source: Finally, our results demonstrated that the heterogeneous development of SC–FC coupling is positively associated with genes in oligodendrocyte-related pathways and negatively associated with astrocyte-related genes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, supported by gene expression analysis in Figure 5.

claim: The heterogeneous development of SC–FC coupling is negatively associated with astrocyte-related genes.
source: Finally, our results demonstrated that the heterogeneous development of SC–FC coupling is positively associated with genes in oligodendrocyte-related pathways and negatively associated with astrocyte-related genes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, supported by gene expression analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Long-range extracortical interconnections among local intracortical microcircuits shape and constrain the large-scale functional organization of neural activity across the cortex.
source: In neural circuitry, long-range (extracortical) interconnections among local (intracortical) microcircuits shape and constrain the large-scale functional organization of neural activity across the cortex (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019; Sarwar et al., 2021; Demirtaş et al., 2019; Deco et al., 2011; Breakspear, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The coupling of structural connectome and functional connectome varies greatly across different cortical regions reflecting anatomical and functional hierarchies.
source: The coupling of structural connectome (SC) and functional connectome (FC) varies greatly across different cortical regions reflecting anatomical and functional hierarchies (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019; Valk et al., 2022; Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2021; Baum et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: SC–FC coupling is regulated in part by genes.
source: The coupling of structural connectome (SC) and functional connectome (FC) varies greatly across different cortical regions reflecting anatomical and functional hierarchies (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019; Valk et al., 2022; Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2021; Baum et al., 2020) and is regulated in part by genes (Valk et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Individual differences in SC–FC coupling relate to cognitive function.
source: The coupling of structural connectome (SC) and functional connectome (FC) varies greatly across different cortical regions reflecting anatomical and functional hierarchies (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019; Valk et al., 2022; Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2021; Baum et al., 2020) and is regulated in part by genes (Valk et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2021), as well as its individual differences relates to cognitive function (Gu et al., 2021; Baum et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The T1w/T2w ratio of MRI has been proposed as a means of quantifying microstructure profile covariance.
source: The T1- to T2-weighted (T1w/T2w) ratio of MRI has been proposed as a means of quantifying microstructure profile covariance (MPC), which reflects a simplified recapitulation in cellular changes across intracortical laminar structure (Valk et al., 2022; Paquola et al., 2019b; Liu et al., 2022; Paquola and Hong, 2023; Park et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: MPC reflects a simplified recapitulation in cellular changes across intracortical laminar structure.
source: The T1- to T2-weighted (T1w/T2w) ratio of MRI has been proposed as a means of quantifying microstructure profile covariance (MPC), which reflects a simplified recapitulation in cellular changes across intracortical laminar structure (Valk et al., 2022; Paquola et al., 2019b; Liu et al., 2022; Paquola and Hong, 2023; Park et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Resting state functional MRI can be used to derive the functional connectome, which captures the synchronization of neural activity.
source: Resting state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) can be used to derive the FC, which captures the synchronization of neural activity (Honey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The communication model is particularly useful because it not only depicts indirect information transmission but also takes into account biodynamic information within acceptable computational complexity.
source: The communication model is particularly useful because it not only depicts indirect information transmission but also takes into account biodynamic information within acceptable computational complexity (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022; Avena-Koenigsberger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most studies have relied on WMC-derived extracortical communications as SC to predict FC, while ignoring the intracortical microcircuits, the MPC.
source: However, most studies have relied on WMC-derived extracortical communications as SC to predict FC, while ignoring the intracortical microcircuits, the MPC.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by inference from the cited studies.

claim: In adults, SC–FC coupling is strongest in sensory cortex regions and weakest in association cortex regions.
source: Previous studies in adults have revealed that the SC–FC coupling is strongest in sensory cortex regions and weakest in association cortex regions, following the general functional and cytoarchitectonic hierarchies of cortical organization (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cortical areas with lower myelination and weaker WM connectivity tend to have more dynamic and complex functional connectivity.
source: This organization may occur due to structural constraints, wherein cortical areas with lower myelination and weaker WM connectivity tend to have more dynamic and complex functional connectivity (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019; Gu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Large-scale association networks emerged over evolution by breaking away from the rigid developmental programming found in lower-order sensory systems.
source: Large-scale association networks emerged over evolution by breaking away from the rigid developmental programming found in lower-order sensory systems (Buckner and Krienen, 2013), facilitating regional and individual specialization (Preti and Van De Ville, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SC–FC coupling is linked to cognitive functions in healthy children, adults, and patients.
source: Furthermore, there is evidence that SC–FC coupling is linked to cognitive functions in healthy children (Chan et al., 2022), adults (Gu et al., 2021; Medaglia et al., 2018), and patients (Kuceyeski et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortical SC–FC coupling is highly heritable.
source: Cortical SC–FC coupling is highly heritable (Gu et al., 2021) and related to heritable connectivity profiles (Valk et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Enhanced myelin thickness in mid-to-deeper layers is specifically associated with the gene expression of oligodendrocytes.
source: For instance, a myeloarchitectural study showed that enhanced myelin thickness in mid-to-deeper layers is specifically associated with the gene expression of oligodendrocytes (Paquola et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The expression levels of genes involved in calcium ion-regulated exocytosis and synaptic transmission are associated with the development of a differentiation gradient.
source: Another functional study found that the expression levels of genes involved in calcium ion-regulated exocytosis and synaptic transmission are associated with the development of a differentiation gradient (Xia et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The study selected 439 participants (5.7–21.9 years of age, 207 males) from the HCP-D dataset.
source: We selected 439 participants (5.7–21.9 years of age, 207 males) in the HCP-D dataset who met our inclusion criteria: available high-quality T1/T2, dMRI, and rs-fMRI data that met the quality control thresholds.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the sample characteristics.

claim: For each participant, multiple connectomes were generated using 210 cortical regions from the Human Brainnetome Atlas.
source: For each participant, we generated multiple connectomes using 210 cortical regions from the Human Brainnetome Atlas (BNA) (Fan et al., 2016), which comprised MPC, WMC, and FC.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the methodology.

claim: Communicability, mean first-passage times of random walkers, and flow graphs (timescales = 1) provided the optimal combination of extracortical connectivity properties for predicting FC.
source: After analysis, we found that communicability (Crofts and Higham, 2009), mean first-passage times of random walkers (Noh and Rieger, 2004), and flow graphs (timescales = 1) provided the optimal combination of extracortical connectivity properties because of significantly predicting FC (p < 0.05, 1000 spin test permutations, Table 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding, supported by Table 1.

claim: Regions with significant SC–FC coupling were located in the middle frontal gyrus, precentral gyrus, paracentral lobule, superior temporal gyrus, superior parietal lobule, postcentral gyrus, cingulate gyrus, and occipital lobe.
source: regions with significant coupling were located in the middle frontal gyrus, precentral gyrus, paracentral lobule, superior temporal gyrus, superior parietal lobule, postcentral gyrus, cingulate gyrus, and occipital lobe (p < 0.05, 1000 spin test permutations, Figure 2B).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: In the visual, somatomotor, default mode and ventral attention networks, SC significantly predict FC variance.
source: In the visual, somatomotor, default mode and ventral attention networks, SC significantly predict FC variance (p < 0.05, 1000 spin test permutations, Figure 2C).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The visual and somatomotor networks had higher coupling values than the other networks.
source: The visual and somatomotor networks had higher coupling values than the other networks (p < 0.05, Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA, Figure 2C).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: There is a negative association between regional distribution of SC–FC coupling and evolution expansion (Spearman's r = −0.52, p < 0.001).
source: Our findings reveal a negative association between regional distribution of SC–FC coupling and evolution expansion (Spearman's r = −0.52, p < 0.001, 1000 spin test permutations, Figure 2D)
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: SC–FC coupling is negatively associated with functional principal gradient (Spearman's r = −0.46, p < 0.001).
source: as well as with the functional principal gradient (Spearman's r = −0.46, p < 0.001, 1000 spin test permutations, Figure 2F).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Nodes exhibiting higher SC–FC coupling tended to exhibit higher myelin content (Spearman's r = 0.49, p < 0.001).
source: Conversely, nodes exhibiting higher SC–FC coupling tended to exhibit higher myelin content (Spearman's r = 0.49, p < 0.001, 1000 spin test permutations, Figure 2E).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Different SCs had preferential contributions to FC variance across cortical regions.
source: Our results demonstrated that different SCs had preferential contributions to FC variance across cortical regions to explain FC variance (p < 0.05, false discovery rate (FDR) corrected, Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA, Figure 2G).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2G.

claim: The SC–FC coupling of most cortical regions increased with age.
source: Regionally, the SC–FC coupling of most cortical regions increased with age (p < 0.05, FDR corrected, Figure 3B)
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Cortical regions with significantly increased SC–FC coupling were located in the frontal lobe, middle temporal gyrus, inferior temporal gyrus, parietal lobe, cingulate gyrus, and lateral occipital cortex.
source: Regionally, the SC–FC coupling of most cortical regions increased with age (p < 0.05, FDR corrected, Figure 3B), particularly that in the frontal lobe, middle temporal gyrus, inferior temporal gyrus, parietal lobe, cingulate gyrus, and lateral occipital cortex.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Cortical regions with significantly decreased SC–FC coupling were located in left orbital gyrus, left precentral gyrus, right superior and inferior temporal gyrus, left fusiform gyrus, left superior parietal lobule, left postcentral gyrus, insular gyrus, and cingulate gyrus.
source: Conversely, cortical regions with significantly decreased SC–FC coupling (p < 0.05, FDR corrected, Figure 3B) were located in left orbital gyrus, left precentral gyrus, right superior and inferior temporal gyrus, left fusiform gyrus, left superior parietal lobule, left postcentral gyrus, insular gyrus, and cingulate gyrus.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: SC–FC coupling significantly predicted individual differences in fluid, crystal, and general intelligence (Pearson's r = 0.3–0.4, p < 0.001, FDR corrected).
source: After controlling for sex, intracranial volume and in-scanner head motion, we found the SC–FC coupling significantly predicted individual differences in fluid, crystal, and general intelligence (Pearson's r = 0.3–0.4, p < 0.001, FDR corrected, Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: After controlling for age, SC–FC coupling remained a significant predictor of general intelligence (Pearson's r = 0.11 ± 0.04, p = 0.01, FDR corrected).
source: Furthermore, even after controlling for age, SC–FC coupling remained a significant predictor of general intelligence better than at chance (Pearson's r = 0.11 ± 0.04, p = 0.01, FDR corrected, Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: SC–FC coupling within the prefrontal, temporal, and lateral occipital lobes was the most predictive of individual differences in general intelligence.
source: Our analysis revealed that SC–FC coupling within the prefrontal, temporal, and lateral occipital lobes was the most predictive of individual differences in general intelligence (Figure 4B).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The weights of frontoparietal and default mode networks significantly contributed to the prediction of general intelligence (p < 0.01, 1000 spin test permutations).
source: In addition, we found that the weights of frontoparietal and default mode networks significantly contributed to the prediction of the general intelligence (p < 0.01, 1000 spin test permutations, Figure 4C).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The gene expression score of the first PLS component explained 22.26% of spatial variance.
source: The gene expression score of the first PLS component (PLS1) explained the most spatial variance, at 22.26%.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: There was a positive correlation (Pearson's r = 0.41, p = 0.006) between the PLS1 score of genes and the spatial pattern of SC–FC coupling development.
source: After correcting for spatial autocorrelation (Vos de Wael et al., 2020), we found a positive correlation (Pearson's r = 0.41, p = 0.006, 10,000 spin test permutations, Figure 5B) between the PLS1 score of genes and the spatial pattern of SC–FC coupling development.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The positive weight genes (364 genes) were prominently enriched for 'myelination', 'monoatomic cation transport', 'supramolecular fibre organization', etc.
source: The positive weight genes (364 genes) were prominently enriched for 'myelination', 'monoatomic cation transport', 'supramolecular fibre organization', etc. (p < 0.05, FDR corrected, Figure 5C).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The negative correlation genes (456 genes) were relatively weakly enriched in 'cellular macromolecule biosynthetic process' and other pathways.
source: The negative correlation genes (456 genes) were relatively weakly enriched in 'cellular macromolecule biosynthetic process' and other pathways (p < 0.05, FDR corrected, Figure 5C).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The genes with positive weights were significantly expressed in oligodendrocytes (75 genes, p < 0.001, permutation test).
source: Our findings showed that the genes with positive weights were significantly expressed in oligodendrocytes (75 genes, p < 0.001, permutation test, Figure 5D).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The genes with negative weights were expressed in astrocytes (43 genes, p < 0.001, permutation test).
source: The genes with negative weights were expressed in astrocytes (43 genes, p < 0.001, permutation test, Figure 5D).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Intracortical microcircuits are interconnected through extracortical WM connections, which give rise to richly patterned functional networks.
source: Intracortical microcircuits are interconnected through extracortical WM connections, which give rise to richly patterned functional networks (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019; Demirtaş et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations to prior literature.

claim: The correspondence between FC and WMC is far from perfect due to the presence of polysynaptic (indirect) structural connections and circuit-level modulation of neural signals.
source: Although many studies have attempted to directly correlate FC with the WMC, this correspondence is far from perfect due to the presence of polysynaptic (indirect) structural connections and circuit-level modulation of neural signals (Sarwar et al., 2021; Baum et al., 2020; Honey et al., 2009; Damoiseaux and Greicius, 2009).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations to prior literature.

claim: Biological models can realistically generate complex structural interconnections, but they have significant temporal and spatial complexity when solving for model parameters.
source: Biological models can realistically generate these complex structural interconnections, but they have significant temporal and spatial complexity when solving for model parameters (Wang et al., 2019; Woolrich and Stephan, 2013; Messé et al., 2015; Honey et al., 2007).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations to prior literature.

claim: Communication models using the WMC integrate the advantages of different communication strategies and are easy to construct.
source: Communication models using the WMC integrate the advantages of different communication strategies and are easy to construct (Avena-Koenigsberger et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: Coupling models that incorporate microarchitectural properties yield more accurate predictions of FC from SC.
source: Coupling models that incorporate these microarchitectural properties yield more accurate predictions of FC from SC (Demirtaş et al., 2019; Deco et al., 2021).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations to prior literature.

claim: SC–FC coupling in association areas, which have lower structural connectivity, was lower than that in sensory areas.
source: SC–FC coupling in association areas, which have lower structural connectivity, was lower than that in sensory areas.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this finding based on the study's results.

claim: This configuration effectively releases the association cortex from strong structural constraints imposed by early activity cascades, promoting higher cognitive functions that transcend simple sensorimotor exchanges.
source: This configuration effectively releases the association cortex from strong structural constraints imposed by early activity cascades, promoting higher cognitive functions that transcend simple sensorimotor exchanges (Buckner and Krienen, 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section states this interpretation with a citation to prior literature.

claim: A macroscale functional principal gradient in the human brain has been shown to align with anatomical hierarchies.
source: A macroscale functional principal gradient (Margulies et al., 2016; Huntenburg et al., 2018) in the human brain has been shown to align with anatomical hierarchies.
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations to prior literature.

claim: SC–FC coupling is dynamic and changes throughout the lifespan.
source: SC–FC coupling is dynamic and changes throughout the lifespan (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022), particularly during adolescence (Valk et al., 2022; Baum et al., 2020)
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations to prior literature.

claim: The two extremes of regions in terms of MPC correlations corresponded to the two anchor points of the gradient.
source: Interestingly, the two extremes of regions in terms of MPC correlations corresponded to the two anchor points of the gradient (Paquola et al., 2019a).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: The preferential regions in WM communication models were consistent with the adult results.
source: The preferential regions in WM communication models were consistent with the adult results (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: In a lifespan study, the global SC–FC coupling alterations with age were driven by reduced coupling in the sensorimotor network.
source: In a lifespan study, the global SC–FC coupling alterations with age were driven by reduced coupling in the sensorimotor network (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: The maturation of the frontoparietal network and default mode network continues into early adulthood.
source: The maturation of the frontoparietal network and default mode network continues into early adulthood, providing an extended window for the activity-dependent reconstruction of distributed neural circuits in the cross-modal association cortex (Buckner and Krienen, 2013).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: The heritability of coupling differs among cortical regions, with higher heritability in the visual network than in other cortical networks.
source: Classic twin studies have reported that the heritability of coupling differs among cortical regions, with higher heritability in the visual network than in other cortical networks (Gu et al., 2021).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: An inverse correlation between the pattern of SC–FC coupling and heritable connectivity profiles has been reported.
source: An inverse correlation between the pattern of SC–FC coupling and heritable connectivity profiles has been reported (Valk et al., 2022).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: Oligodendrocytes play a crucial role in myelination by producing myelin sheaths that enable saltatory conduction and provide metabolic support to axons.
source: Oligodendrocytes, specialized glial cells in the central nervous system, play a crucial role in myelination by producing myelin sheaths that enable saltatory conduction and provide metabolic support to axons (Simons and Nave, 2015).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: Defects in myelination have been linked to developmental disorders.
source: Defects in myelination have been linked to developmental disorders (Berry et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: Significant alterations in SC–FC coupling during development may reflect neural plasticity, such as activity-dependent myelination of axons connecting functionally coupled regions.
source: This seems to indicate that significant alterations in SC–FC coupling during development may reflect neural plasticity, such as activity-dependent myelination of axons connecting functionally coupled regions (Gibson et al., 2014; Mount and Monje, 2017).
evidence: The Discussion section states this interpretation with citations to prior literature.

claim: Both astrocytes and microglia have been implicated in synaptic pruning, a critical developmental process for the formation of fully functional neuronal circuits.
source: Both astrocytes and microglia have been implicated in synaptic pruning, a critical developmental process for the formation of fully functional neuronal circuits that eliminates weak and inappropriate synapses (Kurshan and Shen, 2019; Van Horn and Ruthazer, 2019; Faust et al., 2021).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with citations to prior literature.

claim: The precise establishment of synapses is crucial for establishing the intercellular connectivity patterns of GABAergic neurons.
source: Importantly, the precise establishment of synapses is crucial for establishing the intercellular connectivity patterns of GABAergic neurons (Favuzzi et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion section states this with a citation to prior literature.

claim: The study implemented a conservative quality control procedure to address head motion.
source: First, we implemented a conservative quality control procedure to address head motion, which unavoidably resulted in the loss of some valuable data.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes this methodological choice.

claim: The study applied censoring of high-motion frames and included motion as a covariate in the GLM analysis and cognitive prediction to minimize motion effects.
source: Given the confounding influence of head motion in fMRI studies, especially those involving developing populations, we applied censoring of high-motion frames and included motion as a covariate in the generalized linear model (GLM) analysis and cognitive prediction to minimize its effects (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Ciric et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes this methodological choice with citations.

claim: The reconstruction of short connections between hemispheres is a notable challenge.
source: In addition, the reconstruction of short connections between hemispheres is a notable challenge.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes this limitation.

claim: Changes in gene expression levels during development may introduce bias in the results.
source: Fifth, it is important to acknowledge that changes in gene expression levels during development may introduce bias in the results.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes this limitation.

claim: The study employed an alternative split-half validation strategy and the results supported the reliability of the current findings.
source: To address this, we employed an alternative split-half validation strategy and the results supported the reliability of the current findings.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly describes this validation approach.

claim: The HCP-D dataset comprised 652 healthy participants who underwent multimodal MRI scans and cognitive assessments.
source: The HCP-D dataset comprised 652 healthy participants who underwent multimodal MRI scans and cognitive assessments, and the detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria for this cohort have been described in Somerville et al., 2018.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the dataset with a citation.

claim: All participants or their parents (for participants under the age of 18 years) provided written informed consent and assent.
source: All participants or their parents (for participants under the age of 18 years) provided written informed consent and assent.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the consent process.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Washington University in St. Louis.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Washington University in St. Louis.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the ethical approval.

claim: The MRI data were obtained with a Siemens 3T Prisma with a 32-channel phased array head coil.
source: The MRI data were obtained with a Siemens 3T Prisma with a 32-channel phased array head coil, and detailed imaging parameters are available in Harms et al., 2018.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the imaging equipment with a citation.

claim: The study used the BNA atlas projected on native space.
source: The BNA (Fan et al., 2016) was projected on native space according to the official scripts (http://www.brainnetome.org/resource/) and the native BNA was checked by visual inspection.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the atlas used.

claim: The study reconstructed 14 cortical surfaces from the WM to the pial surface using a robust equivolumetric model.
source: We first reconstructed 14 cortical surfaces from the WM to the pial surface using a robust equivolumetric model (Paquola et al., 2019b; Waehnert et al., 2014).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the surface reconstruction method with citations.

claim: The study used the ball-and-stick model to estimate fibre orientations.
source: Following our previous methodological evaluation study (Feng et al., 2022), the ball-and-stick model estimated from the bedpostx command-line in the FDT toolbox of FSL (https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/fslwiki/FDT) was used to estimate fibre orientations (three fibres modelled per voxel) (Behrens et al., 2003; Jbabdi et al., 2012; Behrens et al., 2007; Hernández et al., 2013).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the diffusion modeling method with citations.

claim: The study used probabilistic tractography to estimate the probability of connectivity between two regions.
source: Next, probabilistic tractography (probtrackx) (Behrens et al., 2007; Hernandez-Fernandez et al., 2019) was implemented in the FDT toolbox to estimate the probability of connectivity between two regions by sampling 5000 fibres for each voxel within each region, correcting for distance, dividing by the total fibres number in source region, and calculating the average bidirectional probability (Feng et al., 2022).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the tractography method with citations.

claim: The study used a consistency-based thresholding approach to remove spurious connections.
source: A consistency-based thresholding approach (weight of the coefficient of variation at the 75th percentile) was used to remove spurious connections, and retain consistently reconstructed connections across subjects (Baum et al., 2020; Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the thresholding method with citations.

claim: The study identified censored frames with motion greater than 0.15 mm.
source: Specifically, we identified censored frames with motion greater than 0.15 mm (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022) based on the Movement_RelativeRMS.txt file.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the motion censoring threshold with a citation.

claim: The study discarded fMRI runs with more than half of the frames flagged as censored frames.
source: We discarded fMRI runs with more than half of the frames flagged as censored frames, and excluded participants with fewer than 300 frames (less than 4 min).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the quality control criteria.

claim: The study used a multilinear model to examine the association of individual nodewise SC profiles with FC profiles.
source: A multilinear model (Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019) was constructed to examine the relationship of individual nodewise SC profiles and FC profiles.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the statistical model with a citation.

claim: The study quantified the nodewise SC–FC coupling as an adjusted coefficient of determination r².
source: For each participant, goodness of fit per node represents the nodal coupling between SC and FC, quantified as the adjusted coefficient of determination (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022)
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the coupling metric with a citation.

claim: The study used Haufe's inversion transform to yield predictor weights of various SCs.
source: Specifically, we used all 27 communication models to predict FC at the node level for each participant. We applied Haufe's inversion transform (Haufe et al., 2014) to obtain predictor weights for each model
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the use of Haufe's transform with a citation.

claim: The study used the Elastic-Net algorithm to predict cognitive performance using nodal SC–FC coupling.
source: Based on our predictive evaluation work (Feng et al., 2022), the Elastic-Net algorithm was applied to predict cognitive performance using nodal SC–FC coupling, which tends to yield robust prediction performance across various dimensions of cognitive tasks.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the prediction algorithm with a citation.

claim: The study employed a nested fivefold cross-validation framework comprising an external CV and an internal CV.
source: We employed a nested fivefold cross-validation (CV) framework comprising an external CV and an internal CV (Feng et al., 2022).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the cross-validation approach with a citation.

claim: The study preprocessed the anatomic and genomic information of the AHBA dataset following a recommended pipeline.
source: We preprocessed the anatomic and genomic information of the AHBA dataset following a recommended pipeline (Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the gene expression preprocessing with a citation.

claim: The study used PLS analysis to mine the linear association between the spatial development pattern of SC–FC coupling and gene expression profiles.
source: PLS analysis (Krishnan et al., 2011) was performed to mine the linear association between the spatial development pattern of SC–FC coupling and gene expression profiles.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the PLS analysis with a citation.

claim: The study performed gene functional enrichment analysis using Metascape.
source: To understand the functional significance of these genes, we performed gene functional enrichment analysis (GO analysis of biological processes and pathways) using Metascape (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the enrichment analysis tool with a citation.

claim: The study assigned genes to 58 cell types derived from five studies focusing on single-cell research using the human postnatal cortex.
source: To investigate the cell type-specific expression of the selected genes, we assigned them to 58 cell types derived from five studies (Zhang et al., 2016; Lake et al., 2018; Habib et al., 2017; Darmanis et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018) focusing on single-cell research using the human postnatal cortex.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the cell type assignment with citations.

claim: The study grouped cell types into seven canonical classes: astrocytes, endothelial cells, excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs.
source: To avoid potential bias in cell-type assignment, we grouped these cell types into seven canonical classes: astrocytes, endothelial cells, excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and OPCs (Seidlitz et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the cell type grouping with citations.

claim: The study computed MPC, SCs, and FC using the multimodal parcellation from the Human Connectome Project (HCPMMP) for reproducibility analysis.
source: To evaluate the robustness of our findings under different parcellation templates, we computed MPC, SCs (WMC, communicability Crofts and Higham, 2009), mean first-passage times of random walkers (Noh and Rieger, 2004), and flow graphs (timescales = 1), and FC using the multimodal parcellation from the Human Connectome Project (HCPMMP) (Glasser et al., 2016).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the reproducibility analysis with a citation.

claim: The study used deterministic tractography with a ball-and-stick model for sensitivity analysis.
source: To evaluate the sensitivity of our results to deterministic tractography, we used the Camino toolbox (http://camino.cs.ucl.ac.uk/) to reconstruct fibres with a ball-and-stick model estimated from bedpostx results (Hernández et al., 2013) and to generate a fibre number-weighted network using the BNA atlas.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the sensitivity analysis with a citation.

claim: The split-half partitioning process was repeated 1000 times to minimize bias due to data partitioning.
source: This process was repeated 1000 times to mitigate any potential bias due to data partitioning.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the validation procedure.
